title: Entry-Level Jobs Shrink 25% as AI Reshapes Hiring for Indian Freshers
excerpt: Automation is pulling away the bottom rung of the career ladder: entry-level IT hiring is down as much as a quarter, GCCs are cutting thousands of roles, and 70% of young Indians say landing a first job is harder than it was three years ago.
body:
• A 2025 EY analysis attributes a 20–25% cut in entry-level IT hiring in India to automation, according to reports; a Nomura survey found 55% of Indian IT firms reduced entry-level hiring, against just 14% for senior roles.
  • Global capability centres are also under pressure: estimates put job cuts at 5,000 to 30,000 this fiscal year, with Cambium Networks shutting its Bengaluru centre in October (around 200 employees) and Hy-Vee closing its India engineering centre in June (around 150), per BusinessLine.
  • An Indeed survey found 70% of young Indians say landing a first job is harder than it was three to five years ago, with 72% saying employers expect prior experience even for entry-level roles and 61% rarely getting a response after applying.
  • What helps: recruiters now prioritise AI, data and cloud skills over degrees (64%, per the Unstop Talent Report 2026); routine testing, basic coding and QA roles are the ones being automated; freshers improve their odds with demonstrated AI fluency, real project portfolios, paid internships, and targeting GCCs, semiconductors and consulting firms, which are still hiring.

The degree is done. The job is not. Across India, a growing number of graduates are discovering that the old contract — study hard, earn a degree, get absorbed by a hiring engine — is breaking down at exactly the point it used to hold: the entry-level job. A 2025 analysis by EY attributed a 20–25% cut in entry-level hiring in India to automation, and the class of 2026 is walking into the aftermath.

The squeeze is not just an IT story, but IT is where it bites hardest. Automation is swallowing the exact tasks that used to be a fresher's first two or three years of work: fixing small bugs, writing test cases, triaging tickets, resolving routine customer queries. India Today reports that students are struggling to land entry-level roles as automation takes over — and the data behind that headline is stark.

What's changing: the bottom rung is being pulled away

Start with the numbers. According to reports on the EY analysis, entry-level IT roles are down 20–25% because of automation. Nomura found 55% of Indian IT firms reduced entry-level hiring, compared with just 14% for senior roles. Stanford researchers found employment for 22–25-year-olds in AI-exposed fields down 13% since generative AI went mainstream.

The Times of India, citing a World Bank report, frames the same shift in white-collar hiring: generative AI has begun hitting entry-level hiring in India as demand for AI skills rises, with job postings declining significantly for roles where AI can serve as a substitute — even as new roles such as AI ethics specialists emerge.

The hiring collapse is visible in the industry's own figures. Staffing data cited in recent reports shows net IT hiring sliding from around 6 lakh in FY22 to roughly 1.4 lakh in FY26. CLSA data shows freshers account for just 13% of active tech openings, and Infosys's share of employees under 30 fell from 60% to 51% in three years. Meanwhile NASSCOM pegs the tech sector at $315 billion in FY26, up 6.1%, with about 135,000 net new jobs — revenue and headcount, once joined at the hip, have quietly separated.

GCCs feel the squeeze too

The global capability centres — long pitched as the new, higher-value absorber of Indian engineering talent — are not immune. BusinessLine reports a string of layoffs and closures: Cambium Networks shut its Bengaluru GCC in October, affecting around 200 employees, and Hy-Vee closed its India engineering centre in June, impacting around 150. Reported reductions also include roughly 200 jobs at PayPal, about 1,500 roles at Visa, and cuts at ServiceNow.

“If the leadership doesn't view the India center as an IP creation or innovation center, there may be full-fledged shutdowns.”

— Gaurav Vasu, CEO and founder of UnearthInsight, quoted by BusinessLine

Industry estimates for GCC job cuts this fiscal year range widely, from around 5,000 to as many as 30,000 roles, against a workforce of 2.4–2.5 million professionals across more than 2,100 centres. Alouk Kumar, founder and CEO of Inductus Group, told BusinessLine that parent-company restructuring and global cost-cutting account for an estimated 50–60% of GCC layoffs, AI-led productivity gains for another 15–20%, and GCC-specific portfolio weakness for 10–15%. Gaurav Vasu estimates more than 400 GCCs could remain under stress over the next few years. Even so, GCCs continue to be the biggest driver of tech hiring in India and could generate around 150,000 new jobs this fiscal year — just not the same kinds of jobs.

The student experience: qualified, experienced — and ignored

An Indeed survey of young Indians puts numbers to the frustration. Seventy percent believe securing a first job is significantly harder than three to five years ago; 72% say employers expect prior experience even for entry-level roles; 61% say they rarely receive a response after applying. The “experience contradiction” — employers wanting candidates who can hit the ground running, from graduates who have never run — is the defining feature of the current market.

The Unstop Talent Report 2026, based on more than 37,000 students and 500 HR leaders, found 85% of engineering students and 84% of undergraduates still unplaced even though 87.8% of HR leaders say they are actively hiring. Only 40% of freshers secure salaries above ₹5 lakh per annum, while 73% expect it. Only 20% of respondents secured a paid internship during their studies, and 43% say financial constraints are limiting their options. Sixty-four percent say repeated rejection has eroded their self-confidence or motivation.

Colleges are adapting on the fly. The National Institute of Technology, Jamshedpur, capped campus recruiter participation at a minimum ₹6 lakh package, since IT firms typically hire in bulk at ₹3.5–4 lakh, professor Saroj Kumar Sarangi told Mint — and he expects GCCs to pick up graduates for skill-based roles, particularly in AI, rather than the traditional software developer positions.

The diaspora angle: the squeeze follows Indian students abroad

The same pressure tracks Indian students overseas. In the US, the Department of Homeland Security has proposed charging international students $70,000 for Optional Practical Training — the work authorization that serves as the bridge from a US degree to a skilled job — up from roughly $500 today, according to Reuters reporting on the proposal, which is now in a 30-day public-comment period. Around 1.44 lakh Indian students participate in OPT, per the Times of India, and Indian student enrolment in the US reportedly fell about 15% in the 2025–26 cycle, according to the Hindu. For families spending lakhs on a US education, the entry-level squeeze at home is increasingly paired with a policy squeeze abroad.

What's next

The jobs are not disappearing so much as mutating. LinkedIn's Grad's Guide 2026 found entry-level hiring in India rose 168% between 2023 and 2025, driven by AI roles, internships and hiring beyond the metros; Naukri recorded fresher hiring up 17% year-on-year in February 2026. The Bernstein equity-research firm wrote to Prime Minister Modi earlier this year warning of an employment crisis as AI threatens white-collar IT jobs — and noted India could need nearly 1 million AI-skilled professionals by 2026, with a large deficit against that number.

“The bottom rung hasn't disappeared. It moved up a few inches and got slipperier. Freshers who climb with judgement and AI fluency will be fine.”

— Abhishek Bartakke, Founder & CEO of Syncro1

The message from recruiters is consistent: stop racing the machine on speed. Compete on judgement, communication and problem framing; build a portfolio that outranks a CGPA; show AI work visibly — how you prompt, verify and improve its output. The old deal — degree in, job out — is gone. The new one is narrower, and it has AI fluency as the gatekeeper.
